children: Japanese smartphone game Monster Strike is set to debut in France, with Koki Kimura, president and CEO of developer Mixi Inc., aiming for its launch in the market by March.

The company is also considering reentry into the U.S. market, Kimura said during an interview with The Yomiuri Shimbun. Mixi's management is mulling the move due to the recent growth in popularity of Japanese anime driven by streaming services. Monster Strike features frequent in-game collaborations with popular anime franchises.
The following is excerpted from the interview.
The Yomiuri Shimbun: Monster Strike has expanded to markets such as India, Hong Kong and Taiwan. Do you have plans to expand further?

Koki Kimura: In terms of population size, we are considering Asia and North America as our targets. In Europe, France is definitely a market we should enter. The country has a strong appreciation for Japanese intellectual property.
Yomiuri: When do you plan to enter the French market?

Kimura: We haven't yet announced a specific timeline, but I hope we can at least launch the game by the end of this fiscal year (ending March 2027). When I visited France, I was surprised to see how highly people respect manga. I felt that the culture of manga is more deeply established there than that of anime. The latest volumes of many Japanese manga have been immediately translated and sold. It's rare to find a country where people read the original manga so enthusiastically. The affection for Japanese content is very strong there.
Yomiuri: If Monster Strike finds success in France, wouldn't it pave the way for reentry into the United States?

Kimura: We have to consider markets on a case-by-case basis. However, the United States also has an enormous appetite for Japanese anime, and its economic scale is massive. The key to reentering the U.S. market is collaboration (with anime franchises). I believe Monster Strike is the game that most frequently features Japanese anime characters from franchises such as Jujutsu Kaisen, Demon Slayer, One Piece and Naruto. We would like to promote Monster Strike with the help of the rights holders of other works as well.
Yomiuri: Did cultural differences in gaming serve as a barrier to success in North America?

Kimura: The game didn't spread as much by word of mouth as it did in Japan. The retention rate wasn't that bad, but when it came to acquiring users through advertising, the cost per user was simply too high, and it just didn't pay off.

The biggest difference from 10 years ago is that we plan to reenter the U.S. market in a format that showcases Japanese anime intellectual property. When a person is looking for a game to play with a friend, they might choose (Monster Strike) if it features a character they are familiar with. Such situations allow the game to spread through word of mouth. While initial advertising costs may be high, the (word-of-mouth) effect ultimately helps us acquire many users.

The growth of video streaming services will be a huge help for us — a big change from 10 years ago. Many people in the United States have now watched Japanese anime. We can use it as a hook to attract users and generate revenue. Pivoting our business model to capitalize on this shift is critical to our reentry into the U.S. market.
